Aplomb

uh-PLOM · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Aplomb is self-confidence or poise, especially when things go wrong.

The intern handled the surprise visit from the company's largest client with such aplomb that no one guessed she had started the job only that morning.

Worked Example

The figure skater fell hard midway through her routine but rose immediately, finished the program with a smile, and even added an extra flourish at the end -- all with such aplomb that the judges gave her bonus points for composure.

Recovering instantly and finishing smoothly, without visible panic or embarrassment, is exactly what aplomb describes: steady self-possession, especially right after something goes wrong.

confidence vs. aplomb

confidence vs. aplomb: Confidence carried him through the first few minutes of the interview, though his hands still trembled slightly under the table.

poise vs. aplomb: Her poise never wavered even once through three hours of hostile cross-examination, leaving the opposing lawyers visibly rattled.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — a-

prefix — a-: according to (French)

root — plomb (plumbum)

root — plomb (plumbum): lead (the metal) (French, from Latin plumbum)

Put it together

Put it together: Aplomb comes from French a plomb, 'according to the plumb line' -- a- ('according to') plus plomb ('lead,' Latin plumbum), the weighted cord builders hang to check that a wall stands perfectly straight. Someone with aplomb stays exactly that steady and upright, even when things go wrong.

Word Choice

Aplomb is a warmly admiring word -- it's almost always used as a compliment for someone who stays impressively composed under pressure, not just for ordinary calm.
